extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetry, literary criticism, and philosophy of mind
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical-literary analysis of the faculties of fancy, imagination, and the law of association as they pertain to poetry, memory, and psychological theory. The page surveys historical positions (Aristotle, Hobbes, Descartes, Hartley) and argues for standards of explanation and method in poetic and psychological enquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fancy and imagination; deduce degree from kind
rubrics_metrics.description: “s purpose to consider the influences of fancy and imagination as they are manifested in poetry, and from the different effects to conclude their diversity in kind; while it is my object to investigate the seminal principle, and then from the kind to deduce the degree.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial aim: map branches (manifestations) to trunk/roots (principles). In studying poetic faculties, identify types (kinds) first, then infer their intensity or degree from that taxonomy. This frames poetic analysis as principled and hierarchical rather than ad hoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity — guard against obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation and paraphrase of Hooker: anticipate and guard against 'complaints of obscurity,' since matters of newness 'seem ... dark and intricate' until the mind grows acquainted with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting difficult theoretical claims (in poetics or philosophy), strive for clarity and provide aids for readers; acknowledge some labour may be required but aim for intelligibility. Use anticipatory statements to mitigate charges of obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present theory as deductions from established premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to 'present an intelligible statement of my poetic creed... not as my opinions, which weigh for nothing, but as deductions from established premises conveyed in such a form as is calculated either to effect a fundamental conviction, or to receive a fundamental confutation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical claims should be grounded in premises that can be examined; formulate arguments so they are capable of producing conviction or being fundamentally refuted. This is a methodological standard for making one’s poetics defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use documents (evidence) for historical/philosophical accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘the accuracy of the statement is to be tried by documents rather than reasoning.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims about intellectual history (priority of ideas, influences between thinkers), prefer documentary/historical evidence (texts, dates, marginalia, provenance) over speculative philosophical argument about who 'discovered' a law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Association — contemporaneity/association principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir James Mackintosh's formulation: 'the law of association as established in the contemporaneity of the original impressions, formed the basis of all true psychology;' Hartley applied this law widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the tendency of contemporaneous impressions to recall one another as a foundational empirical principle in psychology and literary imagination; but subject claims of priority and scope to historical and conceptual scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotle’s five agents/causes of association
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle’s list: (1) connection in time (simultaneous, preceding, or successive), (2) vicinity or connection in space, (3) interdependence or necessary connection (cause and effect), (4) likeness, and (5) contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five relations as the operative conditions by which ideas recall one another. Aristotle’s fuller taxonomy is presented as a more comprehensive and less hypothetical account than later materialist explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association as partial->total recall (Aristotelian formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Ideas by having been together acquire a power of recalling each other; or every partial representation awakes the total representation of which it had been a part.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand memory and passive fancy as mechanisms where fragments evoke the whole context in which they were impressed; this is the working definition of mechanical memory/association in the Aristotelian framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Hartley’s mechanical vibrations hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Hartley’s account posits hypothetical vibrations in an oscillating ether of the nerves as the basis of association; Coleridge argues this is untenable because different external causes cannot plausibly produce the exact same configurative vibration and thus cannot explain associative recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject explanatory models that reduce association to mere propagation of identical material motions. Coleridge offers logical objections (identity of effect from different causes impossible) and thought-experiments to show the insufficiency of purely mechanical hypotheses for mental association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing mind to time-only/material law (limits of mechanicalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: If association is reduced to material atoms subject only to place/time, then phenomena like will and reason would be products of chance temporal proximity and mechanical motion, leading to absurd consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical accounts must preserve the explanatory role of will, reason, and judgment; a law that makes contemporaneity the sole ground of association is both too universal (thus vacuous) and morally/psychologically destructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materialist/mechanical accounts carry unacceptable moral/theological consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If thought and will are mere products of mechanical association, then agency, moral responsibility, and even the idea of God are reduced to 'articulated motions of the air' with corrosive effects on ethics and theology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating philosophical models of mind, consider their wider moral and theological implications. Coleridge argues that theories which nullify agency warrant moral concern and possibly require remedial moral discipline rather than mere argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latent persistence and ordered reliques in memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical claim illustrated by case study: 'reliques of sensation may exist for an indefinite time in a latent state, in the very same order in which they were originally impressed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clinical and historical examples (e.g., feverish reminiscences traced to a caregiver's readings) as evidence that impressions can persist latently and preserve original order — relevant for theories of memory and imaginative recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice, judgment, and selection shape association into memory or fancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge’s program: 'to show, by what influences of the choice and judgment the associative power becomes either memory or fancy; and, in conclusion, to appropriate the remaining offices of the mind to the reason, and the imagination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the transformation from bare associative linkage to distinctive faculties (memory vs. fancy) as dependent on active mental powers (choice, judgment). The presence of purposive mental agency differentiates mere mechanical association from higher mental functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics should examine an author’s own statement before ascribing doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Admonition to critics who 'rendered me ridiculous for a perversion of taste' by attributing strange notions 'on no other authority than their own conjectures'; they 'owe it to themselves as well as to me not to refuse their attention to my own statement of the theory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly/critical practice: do not attribute positions to writers without reading their explicit statements; inspect author's stated theory and grounds prior to judgment or caricature.
